summary: We have developed an interactive web platform aimed at children aged 5 to 10 that features first-person narratives from active or inactive space artifacts and probes left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space. To address the educational challenge, the project personifies scientific hardware, transforming complex missions into accessible stories that explain their original purpose and scientific discoveries. This initiative is vital because it goes beyond basic space education (planets and rockets), emotionally connecting children with real exploration technology. By turning aerospace engineering into captivating storytelling, we foster early scientific curiosity and critical thinking in future generations.
details:
PROJECT DESCRIPTION

What is it?

It is an interactive, educational web platform designed for children aged 5 to 10. Through short, first-person stories—narrated by the objects, probes, and space artifacts themselves that have been left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space—the platform teaches aerospace engineering in an accessible and engaging way.


How does it work?

The platform operates as an interactive web-based environment. Children navigate through visual stories in which individual space objects—such as a Mars rover or a lunar module—come to life, narrating their own missions in the first person. They describe what they discovered and why they remain where they are, transforming complex technical concepts into accessible, adventurous tales.

Innovation and purpose

  • Innovation: Personification of space hardware. Instead of explaining technology from the perspective of adult scientists, technological artifacts tell their own story, generating empathy and natural curiosity in children.
  • Purpose: To connect children's innate fascination with the night sky with the reality of today's space exploration, transcending the basic concept of "just rockets and planets" to value real research technology.

Benefits and Impact

Social, Environmental, and Technological Benefits

  • Social: Promotes digital and educational inclusion in areas outside major urban centers, fostering an early interest in STEM fields among children.
  • Environmental: Raises awareness about the history of space exploration and the management of objects on celestial bodies.
  • Technological: Introduces basic web development tools and digital accessibility concepts to a young audience.

Contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and space missions

  • SDG 4 (Quality Education): Ensures inclusive, equitable, and quality education by promoting opportunities for playful learning about science and technology.
  • SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure): Fosters digital educational innovation and interest in aerospace engineering.
  • Alignment with space missions: Supports the dissemination of information regarding space exploration missions within the community.

Expected impact on the community

Transforming children in Cajamarca—who already enjoy an exceptional night sky—into informed and curious observers, creating a bridge between local observational astronomy and global space technology.

Objectives and Expected Results

General Objective: To develop and deploy an interactive web platform featuring first-person narratives from the perspective of space-related artifacts, designed for children aged 5 to 10.

Expected Results:

  • A functional website hosted on OneCompiler HTML, featuring interactive stories.
  • Increased knowledge and familiarity among children regarding the technological equipment sent into space.
  • Validation of the content with children and parents in the Cajamarca community.

Work Plan

Project Phases and Timeline

  1. Conceptualization Phase: Defining the target audience, selecting space-related subjects (the Moon, Mars, etc.), and establishing a local narrative approach.
  2. Content Creation Phase: Writing first-person stories tailored for children aged 5 to 10.
  3. Web Development Phase: Programming the interactive interface using OneCompiler HTML.
  4. Testing and Launch Phase: Usability validation and project presentation.

Methodology and tools

Tools and software used

  • OneCompiler HTML (web development and deployment environment).
  • Text editing and narrative content design tools.

Programming language and framework

  • Language: HTML (with support for interactive web structure).

Project group

Team:

"COSMIC EXPLORERS"

The team consists of 4 members with clearly defined roles.

Project Location and Setting

Location: Cajamarca, Peru.

Justification for the location: Cajamarca boasts a privileged geographical and atmospheric environment; for much of the year, the night sky offers a clear, unobstructed view of the Moon in all its splendor, along with a vast, star-filled firmament. This naturally sparks the astronomical curiosity of local children, making it the ideal setting to inspire this project.

Justification, Impact, and Conclusions

Relevance and alignment with the mission of exploration

The project aligns with global scientific outreach efforts (such as NASA’s educational objectives) by bringing exploration missions closer to new generations. It demonstrates that space science is not just about distant rockets, but about the active technological legacy left on other worlds.

Conclusions and future improvements

Lessons learned:

The project proves that complex aerospace engineering concepts can be translated into engaging, narrative-driven experiences, and that collaborative teamwork enhances both technical and creative development.

Potential optimizations:

  • Incorporate audio effects and voice-over narration to improve accessibility for young children who are still developing their reading skills.
  • Expand the catalog of space artifacts (including space telescopes and missions to Saturn’s rings).
  • Optimize the design for full compatibility with mobile devices and tablets.
